Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I have to be on guard all the time
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.explanation: The trigger set mixes a socially evaluative trigger ('being seen') with nonspecific discomfort/detachment, while the threat items center on danger from sudden sounds, home intrusion, and interpersonal harm. For a combat trauma profile, 'being seen' is not impossible, but here it is poorly linked to the stated threat pattern and stands out as the one trigger not plausibly connected to the strong Triggers→Threat and Triggers→Negative Appraisals edges.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilance to loud sounds and watching others for danger fit a combat-related threat profile, but specifically monitoring for someone entering the home implies a domestic intrusion threat context that is not supported by the triggers, memory, or appraisals. It pulls the profile toward a different trauma context and weakens cross-node coherence.

vignette:
Kwame's Story

Kwame had been a park ranger for twelve years, long enough to know the names of every trail in the Smoky Mountains, long enough that the work had become something like peace. But peace, he had learned, was conditional. Twenty-three years ago, during his second deployment to Afghanistan, his unit had been ambushed near Kandahar. The convoy had stalled on a narrow mountain road. Kwame was riding in the second vehicle, and the first was hit by an IED. The sound came before understanding-a percussion so absolute it seemed to reorder the world. Smoke, the metallic smell of burning metal and fuel, the screams of men he had trained with. Kwame had returned fire, but the engagement was over in seconds. Three soldiers from the lead vehicle were dead. He had survived without a scratch. The guilt of that fact had never left him.

For years after discharge, Kwame had managed. He married his high school sweetheart, Diane, and they had two daughters now in college. The park ranger work suited him-solitude, structure, the illusion of control. But over the past eighteen months, something had shifted. When a helicopter passed overhead during a patrol, Kwame's entire body would tense. The sound alone-that particular rhythmic thump-could pull him back to that road, and when it did, the boundary between then and now would blur. He found himself on high alert whenever he heard unexpected or loud noises, his jaw clenched, his hand moving instinctively toward his hip. The hypervigilance had become constant. He was certain now that he had to be on guard all the time, that letting his attention slip even for a moment would mean missing the next threat. This conviction had begun to reshape how he moved through the world. When he was at the ranger station, he positioned himself so his back was never fully to a door. On the trail, he watched other hikers with an intensity that made families uncomfortable, scanning their hands, their postures, searching for signs that they might harm him. The discomfort of being around people-the tension in his shoulders, the way his thoughts became scattered and unreal-had become its own trigger. When he felt that creeping detachment, that sensation of being outside his own body, he would leave. He would make an excuse and step away from the visitor center, away from Diane at dinner, away from anything that required him to be fully present.

What frightened him most was what he had become. His memories of that day in Afghanistan were vivid and intrusive, far more real and immediate than ordinary memories. He could smell the burning fuel even now, could taste the dust in his mouth. When these memories surfaced-and they surfaced often, especially when he heard a helicopter or felt that first flutter of disconnection-they would carry with them a crushing certainty: he had permanently changed for the worse. He was no longer the man Diane had married. He was no longer safe to be around. That conviction fed everything else. Because he believed he was damaged beyond repair, the memories felt more urgent, more threatening. And because the memories felt so vivid and real, because they seemed to prove that danger was always imminent, he remained locked in a state of constant vigilance. Every unexpected sound sent him scanning the horizon. Every moment of discomfort made him retreat further into himself, which only deepened his sense of isolation and permanent loss. The guilt compounded it all-he would never forgive himself for not doing more that day, for surviving when three men had not, for the way that survival had warped him into someone he no longer recognized.

Diane had noticed the change. She had tried to reach him, but he had begun declining social invitations, avoiding the places where crowds gathered, making excuses to sleep in the guest room because the intimacy of the bedroom felt like another space he might contaminate with his vigilance. His performance reviews at the park service remained solid, but his supervisor had mentioned that Kwame seemed "distant" with visitors. Last month, when a helicopter had passed during a family hike with his daughters, Kwame had felt the familiar panic rise, and he had simply walked away from them without explanation. He had spent an hour alone on the ridge, waiting for the sound to fade, waiting for the smell of burning metal to leave his nostrils. When he finally returned, his youngest had been crying. That night, Kwame had sat in his truck in the driveway and called a Veterans Affairs clinic. He was forty-six years old, and he could no longer live inside the prison of his own vigilance.
